newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: ISMA delegates look back wistfuly.
newsitem.headline: ISMA delegates look back wistfuly.

text.p: The 29th annual general meeting and conference of the International Securities Market Association (ISMA) ended on Friday with the ISMA board pleased with the two-day event.

However, some older delegates looked back wistfully over the 11 years since the meeting was last held in Singapore in an era when the eurobond arena was a more free-wheeling, and to a great extent unregulated, market.

ISMA Chief Executive John Langton told Reuters after the conference closed he was happy with how the conference had gone. "We've had three diverse presentations with speakers from Singapore, Korea and Australia. I think that shows how international we are."

On Thursday, delegates went through the motions of ISMA's annual general meeting. All proposals put to the floor were passed unanimously and the board's nominations for two new directors and three present directors up for re-election sailed through comortably.
The results of an ISMA survey of its membership were released along with a study of the impact of the euro on the US$25 trillion a year repurchase market.

Only four questions were asked from the floor during a meeting which one seasoned ISMA delegate commented was pretty impressive. "Last year in Cannes, there were none! These meetings have become a bit sterile," he said.
On Friday, delegates heard a speech from Singapore's Finance Minister Richard Hu in which he outlined Singapore's attractions as a regional finance centre.
Former Australian prime minister Paul Keating also addressed the conference, telling delegates the world should make room politically for China.
Walter Imthurn, Executive Director of Hythe Securities in London, was the only one of some 480 delegates who has attended every one of ISMA's 29 annual meetings.

Imthurn was present at the inaugural annual meeting of the Association of International Bond Dealers (AIBD) -- as ISMA was then known -- at the Great Eastern Hotel in London's City financial district.
"There were some 30 firms represented," he told Reuters. This compares with the ISMA's present membership count of around 820.
The eurobond market was then totally unregulated and a tiny fraction of its present size. Secondary market turnover in 1996 totalled some US$15 trillion, ISMA figures show.
Imthurn said the earlier meetings were largely social affairs, but as the threat of regulation from government bodies loomed, things got more serious. "We're in the sober 90's now," he said.
ISMA's Langton agreed. "The days when international liquidity meant how much you could drink in one night are gone. We have a serious role to play," he said.
But Imthurn lamented the fact that delegates have little say on the way things are run now. "The (annual) meeting was the only time you could have a bit of influence," he said.
"Now delegates think 'My job is more important to me than making a fool of myself.' So they keep quiet. That's a pity, they may have valuable input," he said.

Imthurn looked around at the gleaming office towers, shopping complexes and hotels and said, "Look at this area. It didn't exist when the meeting was here 11 years ago. Poor old Raffles (hotel) it's surrounded by tower blocks."
